newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds end lower on profit-taking, dollar firms.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds end lower on profit-taking, dollar firms.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks and bonds closed lower Thursday as investors took profits a day after the Dow Jones industrial average jumped over 8,000 points for the first time ever.
The dollar rose after Japan reported a surprisingly small rise in its politically sensitive trade surplus, and as the weak German mark seemed unlikely to recover soon.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended off 18.11 points to close at 8,020.77, as investors took profits after the previous day's rally pushed the Dow Jones industrial average above 8,000 points for the first time ever.
The Nasdaq index lost 11.78 points to 1,568.85, its first lower finish after 10 straight record highs.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,582 to 1,290 on heavy volume of 629 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"We needed this, we needed room to breathe," said Arnie Owen, managing director of capital markets at Cruttenden Roth. "Right now, things are in the stratosphere."
The Dow's decline came despite a powerful rally by component Merck & Co. Inc. after it reported strong second-quarter results.
The performance was a mirror image of Wednesday's, when the blue-chip average overcame a severe sell-off in component Eastman Kodak Co. after disappointing earnings.
"What we're seeing is investors saying they may sell Kodak because they don't like the earnings or buy Merck because they do," said Richard Cripps chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
"What we're not seeing is evidence that money is leaving the market," he said.
By far the stiffest profit-taking took place in the technology sector, where recent gains have been the most dramatic.

The group may come under new pressure Friday morning, following the release after Thursday's close of Microsoft Corp.'s earnings. Microsoft said it earned 80 cents a share in the quarter, beating Wall Street estimates by a penny.

In the inflation-sensitive bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 5/32, or $1.56 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.49 percent from 6.48 percent at Wednesday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The dollar rose to 116.03 Japanese yen and 1.7937 marks from 115.52 yen and 1.7906 marks late Wednesday.
A forecast for more rain in parched areas of the Midwest this week pushed corn and soybean prices down.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for July delivery closed 7-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $7.74-1/2 and corn for July delivery fell 1 cent a bushel to $2.65-1/2.
July soybeans were also pressured by talk that a major commercial firm would deliver cash soybeans against the contract before it expires July 22.

Wheat prices closed steady, with July futures unchanged at $3.25 a bushel. But traders were perplexed by news during the day of a statement from the Egyptian government barring imports of genetically altered crops.

Gasoline prices at the NYMEX ended sharply higher on concerns that Tropical Storm Danny could disrupt refinery operations in the Gulf of Mexico when supplies of a key gasoline blending component are already tight.
August gasoline settled 1.43 cents higher at 61.89 cents a gallon.
Overseas, London's blue-chip FTSE 100 index finished 15.2 points lower at 4,949.0. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,519.25, up 160.51 points, or 0.79 percent.
